items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: I don't know who told me that, Richard M. Jones or somebody, that they'd heard Bolden say that.

ctx.x: I think it was King Oliver who said that he wanted his band to be able to play so soft they could hear the dancers shuffling.

Yeah, I think that's quoted in Jasmine as a Bolden remark, whether it was, yeah, it was supposed to be a Bolden remark. They say, way down, way down low, so I can hear those whores drag their feet on the floor. I don't know who told me that, Richard M. Jones or somebody, that they'd heard Bolden say that. I don't know whether it's strictly true, but anyway, that was very much the New Orleans tradition. The Ori band followed that.
What was that? Was that for the, part of the form of it, the definite form, or did it build momentum towards the end, or?

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: Williams was enthusiastic about Buddy Bolden

ctx.x: What kind of music do you think they were playing? Would it differ in any way from say what they were playing in the middle 20s?

I would doubt it myself just from the evidence of people's styles not changing that rapidly. I can't, we don't have any records of them. Actually the original Dixieland was the first to record. It might have been of course they always called it ragtime. A lot has been made like for instance in Brun's book on Nick LaRocca always made a big point of that. That they were the first ones to use the word jazz. But not, I'm not trying to say the colored people were first or anything of that kind in this particular case…

You were talking about... Yeah, a lot of the Negroes down here, they're all crazy about him. They all try to imitate him. And yet occasionally you run across some of the old timers that'll say, well, he plays novelty music. It's not really good jazz. Of course, all the young record collectors, and especially, say the ones...

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: we still don't know much about Buddy Bolden, for instance.

ctx.x: I have a record he made with Joe Dierensburg. He might have played a little bit after that, not much.

So, because he, I heard. The LARP record? Yeah. It was made about that time, actually. He had cancer, I heard, at that time. He looked in pretty good health and talked like he'd be playing, like he was alright. But a couple years later, maybe about two years ago, he died. So, evidently he did have cancer. And he was one of the better drummers, not flashy in any way either. And maybe in some sense, monotonous compared to some of the other New Orleans drummers, but still a wonderful rhythm section. Buster Wilson…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: But according to Mineta, Bolden, he was very definite about it, had used a con cornet, too, back in the early 1900s.

ctx.x: So anyway, to get back to the point, Gene Williams had heard these records and agreed with me too that at least Bunk showed some possibilities. You couldn't really tell much how he played, both because his lip wasn't in shape and just by himself. The type of trumpet playing that Bunk did, which was a remarkable thing, and yet by itself it wouldn't sound that effective. Bunk was hardly ever on the beat, so if you didn't hear him patting his foot and all there, you could really tell of course where the beat is, but…
Well, of course, we'll never know what Joe Oliver really sounded like.
